chapterTitle: Godliness With Contentment — The Love of Money, the Good Fight and the Only Sovereign
themeTitle: “But Godliness With Contentment Is Great Gain”

scripture.text: Let as many as are bondservants under the yoke count their own masters worthy of all honor, that the name of God and the doctrine not be blasphemed.
scripture.understanding: ὅσοι εἰσὶν ὑπὸ ζυγὸν δοῦλοι, “as many as are bondservants under the yoke” — the servant family's δοῦλος, a slave who belongs to a master; ζυγός, a yoke, the burden of slavery. Many early believers were slaves. They are to count their δεσπότας, “masters” (the word gives ‘despot’), πάσης τιμῆς ἀξίους, “worthy of all honor,” so that “the name of God and the doctrine not be blasphemed.” Paul addresses believers living inside an existing system; he does not endorse it — he has just condemned ‘slave-traders’ (1:10), and he urges slaves to take freedom if they can (1 Corinthians 7:21). His concern here is the gospel's witness.

scripture.text: Those who have believing masters, let them not despise them, because they are brothers, but rather let them serve them, because those who partake of the benefit are believing and beloved. Teach and exhort these things.
scripture.understanding: Slaves with πιστοὺς δεσπότας, “believing masters,” must not καταφρονείτωσαν, “despise them,” because they are ἀδελφοί, “brothers.” Equality in Christ could tempt a believing slave to show less respect. Instead, μᾶλλον δουλευέτωσαν, “rather let them serve them” better, because those who receive τῆς εὐεργεσίας, “the benefit” of their good service, are πιστοὶ καὶ ἀγαπητοί, “believing and beloved.” Brotherhood transforms the relationship from within. “Teach and exhort these things.”

scripture.text: If anyone teaches a different doctrine, and doesn’t consent to sound words, the words of our Lord Jesus Christ, and to the doctrine which is according to godliness,
scripture.understanding: The false teachers again. εἴ τις ἑτεροδιδασκαλεῖ, “If anyone teaches a different doctrine” — ἕτερος from the ‘another’ family: different in kind (1:3) — καὶ μὴ προσέρχεται ὑγιαίνουσιν λόγοις, “and doesn’t consent to sound words” — healthy words — “the words of our Lord Jesus Christ, and to the doctrine which is according to godliness (εὐσέβειαν).” True teaching agrees with Jesus' words and produces godliness.

scripture.text: he is conceited, knowing nothing, but obsessed with arguments, disputes, and word battles, from which come envy, strife, insulting, evil suspicions,
scripture.understanding: Paul's diagnosis: τετύφωται, “he is conceited” — wrapped in smoke, puffed up (3:6) — μηδὲν ἐπιστάμενος, “knowing nothing,” ἀλλὰ νοσῶν, “but obsessed” — literally ‘sick’, the opposite of the ‘sound’ (healthy) words of verse 3 — περὶ ζητήσεις καὶ λογομαχίας, “with arguments, disputes, and word battles” — λογομαχία is ‘word-fighting’, quarrels over terms. The fruit: φθόνος, “envy”; ἔρις, “strife”; βλασφημίαι, “insulting”; ὑπόνοιαι πονηραί, “evil suspicions” — πονηρός from the evil family: actively harmful.

scripture.text: constant friction of people of corrupt minds and destitute of the truth, who suppose that godliness is a means of gain. Withdraw yourself from such.
scripture.understanding: παραδιατριβαί, “constant friction” — endless wrangling — of people διεφθαρμένων τὸν νοῦν, “of corrupt minds” — rotted through — καὶ ἀπεστερημένων τῆς ἀληθείας, “and destitute of the truth” — robbed of it. Their motive is exposed: νομιζόντων πορισμὸν εἶναι τὴν εὐσέβειαν, “who suppose that godliness is a means of gain” — a way to make money. Religion as a business. “Withdraw yourself from such.”

scripture.text: But godliness with contentment is great gain.
scripture.understanding: Paul turns their slogan around: “But godliness (εὐσέβεια) with contentment (αὐταρκείας) is great (μέγας) gain (πορισμός).” Godliness is indeed great gain — not as a way to get money, but because, combined with contentment, it makes a person truly rich. αὐτάρκεια means self-sufficiency, being satisfied with what one has; the Stoics prized it as independence, but Paul means sufficiency in God (Philippians 4:11).

scripture.text: For we brought nothing into the world, and we certainly can’t carry anything out.
scripture.understanding: The reason: “For we brought (εἰσηνέγκαμεν) nothing into the world (κόσμον), and we certainly can’t carry (ἐξενεγκεῖν) anything out.” The proverbial truth of Job 1:21 and Ecclesiastes 5:15. Every possession is temporary, held between two empty hands. Shrouds have no pockets.

scripture.text: But having food and clothing, we will be content with that.
scripture.understanding: ἔχοντες δὲ διατροφὰς καὶ σκεπάσματα, “But having food and clothing” — σκέπασμα is covering, which can include shelter — τούτοις ἀρκεσθησόμεθα, “we will be content with that.” ἀρκέω, to be enough. Contentment is defined by needs met, not desires satisfied. This is not a ban on owning more, but a heart that does not require more to be at peace.

scripture.text: But those who are determined to be rich fall into a temptation and a snare and many foolish and harmful lusts, such as drown men in ruin and destruction.
scripture.understanding: οἱ δὲ βουλόμενοι πλουτεῖν, “But those who are determined to be rich” — the problem is the will, the settled desire, not wealth itself — ἐμπίπτουσιν εἰς πειρασμόν, “fall into a temptation,” καὶ παγίδα, “and a snare” — a trap — καὶ ἐπιθυμίας πολλὰς ἀνοήτους καὶ βλαβεράς, “and many foolish and harmful lusts,” αἵτινες βυθίζουσιν, “such as drown men” — sink them like a ship going under — εἰς ὄλεθρον καὶ ἀπώλειαν, “in ruin and destruction.”

scripture.text: For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. Some have been led astray from the faith in their greed, and have pierced themselves through with many sorrows.
scripture.understanding: ῥίζα γὰρ πάντων τῶν κακῶν ἐστιν ἡ φιλαργυρία, “For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil.” Note carefully: not money but φιλαργυρία, ‘love of silver’; and ‘a root’ of ‘all kinds of’ evils — κακός from the evil family, bad and harmful things — not the only root of every evil. Some, ὀρεγόμενοι, “in their greed” — reaching out for it, stretching toward it — ἀπεπλανήθησαν ἀπὸ τῆς πίστεως, “have been led astray from the faith,” καὶ ἑαυτοὺς περιέπειραν ὀδύναις πολλαῖς, “and have pierced themselves through with many sorrows” — impaled themselves on their own spears.

scripture.text: But you, man of God, flee these things, and follow after righteousness, godliness, faith, love, perseverance, and gentleness.
scripture.understanding: σὺ δέ, ὦ ἄνθρωπε θεοῦ, “But you, man of God” — the Old Testament title of Moses, Elijah and the prophets. Two commands: φεῦγε, “flee” — run away from — these things (love of money, quarrels, pride), and δίωκε, “follow after,” pursue, chase: δικαιοσύνην, “righteousness”; εὐσέβειαν, “godliness”; πίστιν, “faith”; ἀγάπην, “love” (the love family's ἀγάπη); ὑπομονήν, “perseverance”; πρᾳότητα, “gentleness.” The Christian life is not only running from sin but running toward Christlikeness.

scripture.text: Fight the good fight of faith. Take hold of the eternal life to which you were called, and you confessed the good confession in the sight of many witnesses.
scripture.understanding: ἀγωνίζου τὸν καλὸν ἀγῶνα τῆς πίστεως, “Fight the good fight of faith” — ἀγωνίζομαι and ἀγών, the language of the athletic contest (the root of ‘agony’); καλός from the good family: the noble contest. ἐπιλαβοῦ τῆς αἰωνίου ζωῆς, “Take hold of the eternal life” — grip it, seize it — εἰς ἣν ἐκλήθης, “to which you were called,” καὶ ὡμολόγησας τὴν καλὴν ὁμολογίαν, “and you confessed the good confession,” probably at his baptism or ordination, ἐνώπιον πολλῶν μαρτύρων, “in the sight of many witnesses.”

scripture.text: I command you before God, who gives life to all things, and before Christ Jesus, who before Pontius Pilate testified the good confession,
scripture.understanding: παραγγέλλω σοι, “I command you” — the strongest charge in the letter — before God τοῦ ζῳοποιοῦντος τὰ πάντα, “who gives life to all things” (the WEB follows manuscripts with ζῳοποιέω), and before Christ Jesus, τοῦ μαρτυρήσαντος ἐπὶ Ποντίου Πιλάτου τὴν καλὴν ὁμολογίαν, “who before Pontius Pilate testified the good confession” — when He stood on trial and declared Himself a King whose kingdom is not of this world (John 18:37). Timothy's confession follows his Lord's.

scripture.text: that you keep the commandment without spot, blameless, until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ;
scripture.understanding: The charge: τηρῆσαί σε τὴν ἐντολὴν ἄσπιλον ἀνεπίλημπτον, “that you keep the commandment without spot, blameless” — ἄσπιλος, unstained; ἀνεπίλημπτος, giving no grip to an accuser (3:2) — μέχρι τῆς ἐπιφανείας τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, “until the appearing (ἐπιφάνεια, the shining forth) of our Lord Jesus Christ.” The horizon of faithful ministry is Christ's return.

scripture.text: which in its own times he will show, who is the blessed and only Ruler, the King of kings, and Lord of lords;
scripture.understanding: “which in its own times (καιροῖς ἰδίοις)” — the time family's καιρός: at God's appointed moment, not ours — “he will show (δείξει)” — God will display Christ's appearing. Then a doxology, perhaps from early worship: ὁ μακάριος καὶ μόνος δυνάστης, “the blessed and only Ruler” — δυνάστης, from δύναμις in the power family: the one Sovereign who holds all power. In a world of emperors claiming divinity, God alone is βασιλεὺς τῶν βασιλευόντων, “King of kings,” καὶ κύριος τῶν κυριευόντων, “and Lord of lords.”

scripture.text: who alone has immortality, dwelling in unapproachable light; whom no man has seen, nor can see: to whom be honor and eternal power. Amen.
scripture.understanding: ὁ μόνος ἔχων ἀθανασίαν, “who alone has immortality” — deathlessness belongs to God by nature; creatures receive it only as a gift. φῶς οἰκῶν ἀπρόσιτον, “dwelling in unapproachable light” — light no one can come near (compare Moses, who could see only God's back). “whom no man has seen, nor can see” — God in His essential being is invisible (John 1:18). To Him be τιμὴ καὶ κράτος αἰώνιον, “honor and eternal power” — κράτος from the power family: dominion-strength that prevails. Amen.

scripture.text: Charge those who are rich in this present world that they not be haughty, nor have their hope set on the uncertainty of riches, but on the living God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy;
scripture.understanding: τοῖς πλουσίοις ἐν τῷ νῦν αἰῶνι, “those who are rich in this present world” — αἰών, from the world and time families: ‘this present age’, which is passing. Their riches belong to an age that is ending. παράγγελλε, “Charge” them μὴ ὑψηλοφρονεῖν, “not be haughty” — high-minded, proud — μηδὲ ἠλπικέναι ἐπὶ πλούτου ἀδηλότητι, “nor have their hope set on the uncertainty of riches,” ἀλλ᾽ ἐπὶ θεῷ τῷ ζῶντι, “but on the living God, who richly (πλουσίως) provides us with everything to enjoy (ἀπόλαυσιν).” God is not stingy; He gives richly for enjoyment. The problem is trusting the gifts instead of the Giver.

scripture.text: that they do good, that they be rich in good works, that they be ready to distribute, willing to share;
scripture.understanding: Four commands for the rich: ἀγαθοεργεῖν, “that they do good” — ἀγαθός put into action; πλουτεῖν ἐν ἔργοις καλοῖς, “that they be rich in good works” — καλός: beautiful, noble deeds (both good-family words again, as in 5:10); εὐμεταδότους εἶναι, “ready to distribute” — generous; κοινωνικούς, “willing to share” — fellowship expressed in giving. True wealth is measured by generosity.

scripture.text: laying up in store for themselves a good foundation against the time to come, that they may lay hold of eternal life.
scripture.understanding: The result: ἀποθησαυρίζοντας ἑαυτοῖς θεμέλιον καλὸν εἰς τὸ μέλλον, “laying up in store for themselves a good foundation against the time to come” — echoing Jesus' ‘lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven’ (Matthew 6:20). ἵνα ἐπιλάβωνται τῆς αἰωνίου ζωῆς, “that they may lay hold of eternal life” (some manuscripts read ‘the life that is truly life’). Generosity is not a way to earn salvation but evidence of having grasped real life.

scripture.text: Timothy, guard that which is committed to you, turning away from the empty chatter and oppositions of what is falsely called knowledge;
scripture.understanding: ὦ Τιμόθεε, τὴν παραθήκην φύλαξον, “Timothy, guard that which is committed to you” — παραθήκη is a deposit entrusted to someone's safekeeping, like valuables left with a banker. The gospel is a deposit to be guarded, not altered. ἐκτρεπόμενος τὰς βεβήλους κενοφωνίας, “turning away from the empty chatter” — κενοφωνία, empty sounds — καὶ ἀντιθέσεις τῆς ψευδωνύμου γνώσεως, “and oppositions of what is falsely called knowledge” — γνῶσις from the know family, ‘knowledge’ falsely so called. Some later teachers called themselves ‘Gnostics’ from this word.

scripture.text: which some profess, and thus have wandered from the faith. Grace be with you. Amen.
scripture.understanding: ἥν τινες ἐπαγγελλόμενοι, “which some profess” — claiming this ‘knowledge’ — περὶ τὴν πίστιν ἠστόχησαν, “and thus have wandered from the faith” — ἀστοχέω, missed the mark, the archer's word from 1:6. The letter ends where it began: some have missed the target. Then: ἡ χάρις μεθ᾽ ὑμῶν, “Grace be with you” — plural, ‘you all’: the letter was meant for the whole church.

visualMeditations.title: Shrouds Have No Pockets
visualMeditations.image: Picture a newborn baby in a midwife's arms: naked, empty-handed, owning nothing. Now picture an old man on his deathbed in Ephesus. He spent his life accumulating land, silver and slaves. His relatives are already arguing in the next room about who will inherit what. He dies, and they wrap his body in a linen shroud. It has no pockets. Everything he gathered stays behind. Then picture a poor believer who has food, clothing and a heart at rest in God. She dies too — but she goes into eternity rich.
visualMeditations.meaning: Paul writes, “But godliness with contentment is great gain. For we brought nothing into the world, and we certainly can’t carry anything out. But having food and clothing, we will be content with that” (vv. 6–8). Contentment is not resignation; it is the settled peace of knowing God is enough. Jesus warned, “a man’s life doesn’t consist of the abundance of the things which he possesses” (Luke 12:15). The question is not how much you have, but whether you can be at rest with what God provides.

visualMeditations.title: The Self-Inflicted Wounds
visualMeditations.image: Picture a man reaching desperately for a bag of gold hanging just out of reach on a wall of spikes. He stretches, strains and lunges. Each time he grabs at it, he is cut by the spikes around it. His arms bleed, his clothes tear, but he keeps reaching. Finally he gets the bag — and finds himself pierced in a dozen places, alone, his family gone, his faith abandoned, his peace destroyed. He did not mean to wound himself. He only wanted more.
visualMeditations.meaning: “But those who are determined to be rich fall into a temptation and a snare and many foolish and harmful lusts, such as drown men in ruin and destruction. For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. Some have been led astray from the faith in their greed, and have pierced themselves through with many sorrows” (vv. 9–10). Money itself is not evil; the love of it is a root from which many kinds of evil grow. Watch for the reaching heart, the restless stretching toward more.

visualMeditations.title: Flee, Pursue, Fight
visualMeditations.image: Picture a young soldier on a battlefield. Behind him, enemies he must not engage are trying to lure him into an ambush: greed, quarrels, pride. He runs from them. Ahead of him is a prize, and he runs toward it with all his strength: righteousness, godliness, faith, love, endurance, gentleness. Then the real battle begins, and he plants his feet and fights — not against people, but for the faith entrusted to him, gripping eternal life with both hands. Behind him stand many witnesses who heard him confess Christ, and above him the King who once made the same good confession before Pilate.
visualMeditations.meaning: “But you, man of God, flee these things, and follow after righteousness, godliness, faith, love, perseverance, and gentleness. Fight the good fight of faith. Take hold of the eternal life to which you were called” (vv. 11–12). The Christian life has three verbs: flee, pursue, fight. Some things you must run from; some you must chase; and the faith itself you must defend with everything you have. Paul did it to the end: “I have fought the good fight. I have finished the course. I have kept the faith” (2 Timothy 4:7).

structure.label: Slaves and Masters (v. 1-2)
structure.body: Believing slaves should honour their masters so that God's name and the teaching are not slandered, and serve believing masters all the better because they are beloved brothers; Timothy must teach and urge these things.

structure.label: False Teachers and the Love of Money (v. 3-10)
structure.body: Anyone teaching a different doctrine is conceited and diseased with controversies that produce envy, strife and suspicion, imagining godliness is a means of gain; but godliness with contentment is great gain, since we bring nothing in and take nothing out; those who want to be rich fall into temptation and ruin, for the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil.

structure.label: The Charge to the Man of God (v. 11-16)
structure.body: Timothy must flee these things and pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, endurance and gentleness; fight the good fight of faith and take hold of eternal life; and keep the commandment unstained until the appearing of Christ, whom God will display in His time — the blessed and only Sovereign, King of kings and Lord of lords, immortal and dwelling in unapproachable light.

structure.label: A Charge to the Rich (v. 17-19)
structure.body: The rich must not be proud or trust uncertain riches but God, who richly provides everything to enjoy; they must do good, be rich in good works, generous and ready to share, storing up a good foundation for the future so that they take hold of real life.

structure.label: Guard the Deposit (v. 20-21)
structure.body: Timothy must guard what has been entrusted to him, avoiding godless chatter and the contradictions of what is falsely called knowledge, by which some have swerved from the faith. Grace be with you all.

sections.heading: Godliness Is Not a Business
paragraphs: The final chapter begins with instructions to believing slaves (vv. 1–2). Slavery was woven into the Roman economy, and many early Christians were slaves. Paul tells them to honour their masters “that the name of God and the doctrine not be blasphemed” (v. 1). This must be read honestly: Paul is addressing how believers live faithfully within a system they could not change, not endorsing that system. In the same letter he lists ‘slave-traders’ among the lawless (1:10), and elsewhere he writes, “if you get an opportunity to become free, use it” (1 Corinthians 7:21), and tells masters to give their servants “that which is just and equal” (Colossians 4:1). The gospel's principle that “there is neither slave nor free man” (Galatians 3:28) would eventually undermine the institution itself.

Then Paul returns to the false teachers and exposes their roots. They do not agree with “sound words, the words of our Lord Jesus Christ, and to the doctrine which is according to godliness” (v. 3). Instead they are “conceited, knowing nothing, but obsessed with arguments, disputes, and word battles” (v. 4). The fruit of their teaching is ugly: envy, strife, insults, evil suspicions and constant friction. And their motive is money: they “suppose that godliness is a means of gain” (v. 5). Religion had become a business.

Paul takes their slogan and turns it inside out: “But godliness with contentment is great gain” (v. 6). Godliness is gain — but not financial gain. Combined with contentment, it makes a person truly rich. The reason is simple: “For we brought nothing into the world, and we certainly can’t carry anything out. But having food and clothing, we will be content with that” (vv. 7–8). Paul had learned this personally: “I have learned in whatever state I am, to be content in it” (Philippians 4:11). Hebrews adds the foundation of contentment: “Be free from the love of money, content with such things as you have, for he has said, ‘I will in no way leave you, neither will I in any way forsake you’” (Hebrews 13:5).

sections.heading: A Root of All Kinds of Evil
paragraphs: Paul warns those who are not content: “But those who are determined to be rich fall into a temptation and a snare and many foolish and harmful lusts, such as drown men in ruin and destruction” (v. 9). The issue is the determination, the settled desire, to be rich. That desire becomes a trap. Then the famous verse: “For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. Some have been led astray from the faith in their greed, and have pierced themselves through with many sorrows” (v. 10). Notice what Paul does not say: money is not evil, and the love of money is not the only cause of every sin. But it is a root from which many kinds of evil grow.

Jesus taught the same: “No one can serve two masters … You can’t serve both God and Mammon” (Matthew 6:24), and “Beware! Keep yourselves from covetousness, for a man’s life doesn’t consist of the abundance of the things which he possesses” (Luke 12:15). The rich fool built bigger barns, but God said, “You foolish one, tonight your soul is required of you” (Luke 12:20). Greed does not only harm others; it pierces the greedy person with many sorrows.

Against this, Paul charges Timothy: “But you, man of God, flee these things, and follow after righteousness, godliness, faith, love, perseverance, and gentleness. Fight the good fight of faith. Take hold of the eternal life to which you were called” (vv. 11–12). Flee, pursue, fight. The strength for this comes from looking at Christ, “who before Pontius Pilate testified the good confession” (v. 13), and at His coming appearing. Paul bursts into worship of God, “the blessed and only Ruler, the King of kings, and Lord of lords; who alone has immortality, dwelling in unapproachable light” (vv. 15–16). Next to that King, money looks very small.

sections.heading: Rich Toward God
paragraphs: Not all the Ephesian believers were poor; some were wealthy. Paul does not tell them to give everything away, but he charges them: “Charge those who are rich in this present world that they not be haughty, nor have their hope set on the uncertainty of riches, but on the living God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy” (v. 17). Two dangers attend wealth: pride and false security. And there is a beautiful truth here: God “richly provides us with everything to enjoy.” He is not a miser. The problem is not enjoying His gifts but trusting them instead of Him.

Then the positive command: “that they do good, that they be rich in good works, that they be ready to distribute, willing to share; laying up in store for themselves a good foundation against the time to come, that they may lay hold of eternal life” (vv. 18–19). The rich are to become rich in a different currency — good works and generosity. This echoes Jesus: “but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust consume” (Matthew 6:20), and His warning about the one who “lays up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God” (Luke 12:21).

The letter closes with a final charge: “Timothy, guard that which is committed to you, turning away from the empty chatter and oppositions of what is falsely called knowledge; which some profess, and thus have wandered from the faith” (vv. 20–21). The gospel is a deposit entrusted to Timothy, to be guarded, not improved. The false teachers claimed special knowledge; Paul calls it ‘falsely called knowledge’. Some ‘missed the mark’ — the same archer's word as 1:6. The letter ends where it began: guard the truth, aim at love and godliness. And the final word is grace: “Grace be with you.”

ntConnection.heading: Money, Contentment and the King of Kings
paragraphs: Jesus' teaching on money underlies this chapter. “Don’t lay up treasures for yourselves on the earth, where moth and rust consume, and where thieves break through and steal” (Matthew 6:19). “How difficult it is for those who have riches to enter into God’s Kingdom!” (Mark 10:23). And Paul himself reminded the Ephesian elders of Jesus' words: “It is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts 20:35). Contentment is possible because God has promised, “I will in no way leave you, neither will I in any way forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5).

The ‘good confession’ of Jesus before Pilate appears in the Gospels: “Pilate therefore said to him, ‘Are you a king then?’ Jesus answered, ‘You say that I am a king. For this reason I have been born, and for this reason I have come into the world, that I should testify to the truth’” (John 18:37). Timothy's confession of faith follows the pattern of his Lord's.

The doxology of verses 15–16 resonates with Revelation, where the Lamb “is Lord of lords, and King of kings” (Revelation 17:14) and bears the name “KING OF KINGS, AND LORD OF LORDS” (Revelation 19:16). And the invisibility of God is explained in John: “No one has seen God at any time. The one and only Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him” (John 1:18). The God who dwells in unapproachable light has made Himself known in Christ.

lexicon.insight: Strong's: “self-satisfaction, i.e. (abstractly) contentedness, or (concretely) a competence.” The Stoic philosophers used it for self-sufficiency, needing nothing from outside. Paul transforms it: Christian contentment is not self-sufficiency but God-sufficiency. The related adjective appears in Philippians 4:11: ‘I have learned in whatever state I am, to be content in it.’ Paul uses the noun in 2 Corinthians 9:8 of God giving all sufficiency in all things. Contentment is a learned trust that God is enough.

Strong's: “avarice.” Literally ‘love of silver’ (φίλος + ἄργυρος). It appears only here in the New Testament; the related adjective describes the Pharisees as ‘lovers of money’ (Luke 16:14). Paul does not say money is evil, but that the love of it is a root of all kinds of evils. Money is a good servant and a terrible master. The test is not how much you have, but what you love and trust.

Strong's: “to struggle, literally (to compete for a prize), figuratively (to contend with an adversary), or genitive case (to endeavor to accomplish something).” It gives us ‘agonise’. Paul uses it of Epaphras wrestling in prayer (Colossians 4:12) and of his own ministry (Colossians 1:29). ‘Fight the good fight of faith’ pictures an athlete or soldier giving full effort. The Christian life is not passive drifting; it is an all-out contest for faith, with eternal life as the prize already given and to be grasped.

Strong's: “a ruler or officer.” From δύναμαι, to be able, related to δύναμις in the power family: one who holds power. It is used of the Ethiopian court official (Acts 8:27) and of rulers brought down by God (Luke 1:52). Here God is ‘the blessed and only Ruler’: every other ruler holds power temporarily and on loan. In a city where the emperor claimed divine honours, Paul confesses that there is only one true Sovereign.

Strong's: “a deposit, i.e. (figuratively) trust.” It describes valuables entrusted to someone for safekeeping, to be returned intact. The gospel is not Timothy's to change; it is a deposit from God to be guarded faithfully. Paul uses the same word twice in 2 Timothy (1:12, 14). Every generation of believers receives the same deposit and must hand it on unchanged. Guarding it means both holding to it and living it.

holySpiritRevelation.intro: The Spirit is dealing with three things in this chapter: your relationship with money, the direction you are running, and the treasure you are guarding.

items.title: What Are You Reaching For?
items.body: The love of money often hides behind good reasons: security, family, opportunity. The Spirit asks: what are you reaching for? Is there a restless desire for more that is pulling you away from faith, peace or generosity? Ask Him to expose any love of money in your heart and to teach you contentment — the settled trust that, with food and clothing and God's presence, you have enough.

items.title: Flee, Pursue, Fight
items.body: Paul gives Timothy three verbs. The Spirit may be showing you something to flee — a temptation you keep flirting with. He may be calling you to pursue a virtue you have neglected — gentleness, endurance, love. And He may be calling you to fight for your faith in a season of pressure or doubt. Ask Him which verb is most urgent for you this week, and act on it.

items.title: Rich Toward God
items.body: If you have more than you need, the Spirit is not condemning you, but He is calling you: do good, be rich in good works, be generous and ready to share. God richly provides everything for your enjoyment, and also so that you can bless others. Ask Him where your generosity should flow this month, and lay up treasure that lasts.

audit.title: The Contentment Check
audit.body: Finish this sentence honestly: ‘I would be content if I had …’ If the answer is more than food, clothing and God (v. 8), ask God to show you where your heart is reaching too far.

audit.title: The Root Check
audit.body: Look at your spending, saving and giving over the last month. Do they reveal love of money, or trust in God (vv. 9–10, 17)? Name one change you will make.

audit.title: The Deposit Check
audit.body: What has God entrusted to you — the gospel, a family, a ministry, gifts, resources (v. 20)? Are you guarding these faithfully? Write down one way you will guard or use one of them better.

practices.title: A Generosity Experiment
practices.body: For one month, practise verses 18–19. Set aside a specific amount — larger than feels comfortable — to give away. Look for needs: a struggling family, a missionary, a widow, a ministry. Give quietly. Also give time: do one practical good work each week. At the end of the month, write down what God taught you about contentment, trust and joy through giving.

practices.title: Learn the Doxology
practices.body: Memorise verses 15–16: “the blessed and only Ruler, the King of kings, and Lord of lords; who alone has immortality, dwelling in unapproachable light; whom no man has seen, nor can see: to whom be honor and eternal power. Amen.” Speak it aloud each morning for a week, especially when you feel anxious about money or the future. Let worship of the true Sovereign shrink the power of wealth over your heart.

prayerReflection: “Blessed and only Sovereign, King of kings and Lord of lords, You alone have immortality and dwell in unapproachable light. Let my life honour You and not bring blasphemy on Your name. Keep me from conceit, quarrels over words, envy, strife and evil suspicion. Keep me from ever treating godliness as a means of gain. Teach me that godliness with contentment is great gain. I brought nothing into the world and I will take nothing out; with food and clothing and You, I have enough. Uproot every love of money in me, and keep me from the snares and sorrows of greed. Make me flee these things and pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, endurance and gentleness. Help me fight the good fight of faith and take hold of eternal life. Keep me faithful, unstained and above reproach until the appearing of my Lord Jesus Christ. Where You have given me more than I need, make me humble, hopeful in You alone, rich in good works, generous and ready to share. Help me guard the gospel You have entrusted to me. Grace be with me and all Your people. In the mighty name of Jesus, Amen!”

storyConnections.title: The Rich Fool
storyConnections.summary: A man asked Jesus to make his brother share an inheritance. Jesus refused and warned, “Beware! Keep yourselves from covetousness, for a man’s life doesn’t consist of the abundance of the things which he possesses” (Luke 12:15). Then He told of a rich man whose land produced a huge harvest. He decided to tear down his barns and build bigger ones, and said to himself that he could take his ease, eat, drink and be merry for many years. “But God said to him, ‘You foolish one, tonight your soul is required of you. The things which you have prepared—whose will they be?’” (Luke 12:20). Jesus concluded: “So is he who lays up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God” (Luke 12:21). 1 Timothy 6 gives the same warning and the same remedy.

storyConnections.title: Jesus' Good Confession Before Pilate
storyConnections.summary: Pilate summoned Jesus and asked if He was the King of the Jews. Jesus answered that His kingdom was not of this world; if it were, His servants would fight. “Pilate therefore said to him, ‘Are you a king then?’ Jesus answered, ‘You say that I am a king. For this reason I have been born, and for this reason I have come into the world, that I should testify to the truth. Everyone who is of the truth listens to my voice’” (John 18:37). Pilate asked, ‘What is truth?’ and went out. Facing death, Jesus confessed the truth calmly and faithfully. Paul points Timothy to this ‘good confession’ as the model for his own unwavering witness.

storyConnections.title: Zacchaeus Gives Half His Goods
storyConnections.summary: Zacchaeus was a chief tax collector in Jericho, rich and despised. When Jesus came through, he climbed a sycamore tree to see Him, and Jesus called him by name and invited Himself to his house. People grumbled that Jesus was going to be the guest of a sinner. But Zacchaeus stood and said he would give half his goods to the poor, and if he had cheated anyone, he would repay four times as much. Jesus declared that salvation had come to his house, because the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost. Zacchaeus shows what happens when a rich man stops hoping in uncertain riches and puts his hope in God: he becomes rich in good works, ready to share.
